title: The right wing bleeds
subtitle: Corps on the wheel — 1st, 2nd and 3rd Armies — from the assembly to the Marne

start.note: Sixteen corps on the wheel as the advance began: six in the 1st Army (II, III, IV, IX, III Reserve, IV Reserve), six in the 2nd (Guard, VII, X, Guard Reserve, VII Reserve, X Reserve), four in the 3rd (XI, XII, XIX, XII Reserve) — with the IX Reserve Corps still held in Schleswig.

entries.label: III Reserve Corps left before Antwerp
entries.note: As the 1st Army passed Brussels the III Reserve Corps turned off to mask the Belgian field army in Antwerp; it never rejoined the wheel.

entries.label: VII Reserve Corps invests Maubeuge
entries.note: The fortress held until 7 September; the corps reached the front only after the Marne was lost.

entries.label: First sortie from Antwerp: the III Reserve Corps pinned north of Brussels
entries.note: Nothing leaves the ledger, but the corps that has already left cannot come back: the Belgian field army comes out towards Malines and Louvain and the III Reserve Corps, with the IX Reserve Corps arriving behind it, is kept facing north.

entries.label: Guard Reserve and XI Corps entrain for East Prussia
entries.note: Moltke's decision of 25 August, taken when the West seemed won and East Prussia lost; the corps were in transit during Tannenberg and missing from the gap at the Marne.

entries.label: IX Reserve Corps arrives from Schleswig
entries.note: Released once a British landing on the North Sea coast was ruled out; it relieved the III Reserve Corps before Antwerp for a while and reached the Ourcq only on 8–9 September.

entries.label: The Marne: what is left on the wheel
entries.note: Thirteen corps nominally, twelve in the battle — the 1st Army's five, the 2nd's four, the 3rd's three — against a French left that had been reinforced from Lorraine by rail and a new army at Paris.

entries.label: Maubeuge surrenders — the VII Reserve Corps is free, too late
entries.note: Thirteen days for a fortress the plan had not counted on; the corps marches for the front the next day, as the right wing is already being turned on the Ourcq.

entries.label: Second sortie from Antwerp: a reserve division turned back north
entries.note: The 6th Reserve Division, on its way south, and a division of the XV Corps from Alsace are drawn to Brussels instead — nothing the Marne could still have used, but troops the Aisne would have.

entries.label: VII Reserve Corps reaches the Chemin des Dames — a day after the Marne
entries.note: Zwehl's corps comes back on to the ledger after a sixty-kilometre march in a day and a night, and fills the gap between the 1st and 2nd Armies on the Aisne ridge just as the BEF climbs towards it. Had Maubeuge fallen as fast as Namur, it would have been there for the Marne.

comparisons.label: The 1905 memorandum: right wing to left
comparisons.note: Schlieffen's paper put almost everything north of Metz — a ratio usually quoted as about seven to one; Zuber objects that many of those divisions existed only on paper.

comparisons.label: Moltke's August 1914 deployment
comparisons.note: The left wing in Lorraine and Alsace strengthened to meet a real French offensive: about three to one.

comparisons.label: Mid-August: the six Ersatz divisions go to Lorraine
comparisons.note: The last reserve of the deployment went to the left, not the wheel; Moltke's defenders answer that the French Plan XVII offensive made it necessary.

summary: The plan's logic was weight on the right; the campaign's arithmetic was the weight leaving it. Before a shot was fired at the Marne the wheel had given up a corps to Antwerp, a corps to Maubeuge and two corps to East Prussia — the decision point of 25 August — and received one back from Schleswig.[^herwig-2009] [^reichsarchiv-weltkrieg-1] Whether the missing corps would have closed the gap, and whether Moltke's thickened left was prudence or betrayal of the concept, is the argument between Mombauer and Herwig on one side and Zuber on the other.[^mombauer-2001] [^zuber-2002]

title: The left wing grows — by rail
subtitle: Corps Joffre moved west from Lorraine and Alsace by train, 20 August – 4 September

start.note: Interior lines: the French railway net let Joffre move a corps from Lorraine to Paris in two days while the German corps walked.

entries.label: XVIII Corps to the 5th Army on the Sambre
IX Corps to the 4th Army
entries.note: From the 2nd Army, 22–24 August; later Foch's 9th Army.

entries.label: VII Corps to Amiens — the 6th Army forms
entries.note: From Alsace, 25–27 August, under Instruction générale no 2.

entries.label: 55th and 56th Reserve Divisions to Paris
entries.note: From the Army of Lorraine, 27–29 August; the divisions that opened the Ourcq.

entries.label: IV Corps to Paris
entries.note: From Verdun, 2–4 September; part of its 7th Division reached the front by taxi.

summary: Schlieffen's wheel assumed the French would not be able to shift their weight faster than the Germans could march. They could: between Instruction générale no 2 and the Marne Joffre moved the equivalent of five corps from the right to the left by rail, built a new army at Amiens and Paris, and reinforced the 5th — interior lines against exterior lines, the railway against the boot.[^afgg-1-1] [^herwig-2009] [^strachan-2001]
